questions.q: What do the letters of the LEARN complaint-handling model stand for?
questions.explain: Topic 8: LEARN = Listen, Empathize, Apologize, React, Notify (inform the guest and colleagues so the problem is not repeated).

questions.q: The idea that a guest whose problem was solved very well may become more loyal than a guest who had no problem is called…
questions.explain: Topic 8: the service recovery paradox shows why complaints are an opportunity, not only a problem.

questions.q: When handling a complaint, staff should first find out who is to blame before apologising for the inconvenience.
questions.explain: Topic 8: staff should apologise for the inconvenience even before the cause is clear, and never blame the guest or colleagues.

questions.q: A caller says she is a guest's wife and asks for his room number. What is the ethical response of the receptionist?
options: Give the number, because family members have a right to know
Say loudly that the guest is not in the hotel
Ask her to come to the hotel and then show her the guest list
Offer to connect the call to the room or take a message, without revealing the number
questions.explain: Topic 9: privacy rules forbid revealing room numbers or confirming a stay to third parties; connecting the call protects the guest.

questions.q: Which actions are part of ethical handling of overbooking ("walking" a guest)?
options: Arranging a comparable or better hotel nearby
Paying for the first night and transport
Choosing the guest who looks least likely to complain
Warning the guest early when possible
questions.explain: Topic 9: ethical overbooking means early warning, a comparable room elsewhere and covering costs, using fair criteria — not targeting 'weak' guests.

questions.q: A hotel shows a low price on its website and adds a compulsory resort fee only at the last booking step. This practice is called…
questions.explain: Topics 9 and 12: drip pricing hides compulsory fees until the end of the booking, which misleads guests.

questions.q: A supplier offers a hotel purchasing manager a personal payment for choosing his products. What is this situation?
options: A conflict of interest that should be refused and reported
A gratuity that the manager may keep
questions.explain: Topic 10: money or expensive gifts from suppliers create a conflict of interest (or bribery) and must be refused.

questions.q: Which statements about tips, gifts and service charges follow workplace ethics?
options: Tip distribution (individual or pooled) must be transparent and fair
A service charge should be clearly shown to guests
Managers may keep all tips because they are responsible for the team
Small gifts from guests are declared according to company policy
questions.explain: Topic 10: tips must be shared by a fair, transparent policy, service charges shown clearly and small gifts declared; managers taking staff tips is unfair.

questions.q: Which leadership approach puts serving and developing employees first (Robert Greenleaf)?
questions.explain: Topic 11: in servant leadership the leader serves staff; well-treated staff in turn serve guests better.

questions.q: "Tone at the top" refers to the ethical example set by senior management.
questions.explain: Topic 11: leaders who act with integrity create an ethical climate; employees copy what managers do, not only what they say.

questions.q: A hotel calls itself an "eco-hotel" in advertising but has no real environmental measures. This is…
questions.explain: Topics 12 and 14: greenwashing means presenting a business as more environmentally friendly than it really is.

questions.q: Which practices are unethical in managing online reviews?
options: Writing fake positive reviews about your own hotel
Replying politely to a negative review and explaining what was changed
Rewarding guests only for positive reviews
Deleting or hiding honest negative reviews
questions.explain: Topic 12: fake reviews, paying only for positive reviews and hiding criticism are unethical; polite replies are good practice.

questions.q: Which quick ethics test asks: "Would I be comfortable if this decision appeared in the news or on social media?"
questions.explain: Topic 13: the newspaper test checks whether a decision could be defended publicly.

questions.q: When analysing an ethical case, it is enough to consider the short-term profit of the hotel.
questions.explain: Topic 13: a good analysis considers all stakeholders (guests, staff, owners, community) and long-term effects; looking only at short-term profit is a common mistake.

questions.q: What are the four levels of Carroll's CSR pyramid, from bottom to top?
questions.explain: Topic 14: Carroll's pyramid — economic (profitable), legal (obey the law), ethical (be fair), philanthropic (good corporate citizen).

questions.q: Which is correct etiquette when serving a guest who uses a wheelchair and is accompanied by a friend?
options: Speak to the guest directly and ask before helping
Speak only to the friend, because it is faster
Push the wheelchair without asking to save the guest effort
Avoid eye contact so the guest does not feel uncomfortable
questions.explain: Topic 15: speak directly to the guest, ask 'May I help you?' and never move a wheelchair without permission.
